rewrites.prompt: In March a Windhoek furniture shop sells N$60 000 of goods, all on 60-day credit, and receives no other money. Its costs for the month, all paid in March, are N$45 000. Explain the difference between the shop's net cash flow for March and the profit it earned in March.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Net cash flow is the cash received in a month less the cash paid out in it; profit is the revenue of the month less its costs, whether or not the money has moved. For the shop, the N$60 000 of credit sales are March revenue but bring in no cash until May. So March shows a profit of N$15 000 and, in the same month, a net cash flow of minus N$45 000. The boundary is when the money moves against when the trade happens, which is why a negative net cash flow in March is not evidence that the shop made a loss.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - net cash flow counts money received and paid in the month, profit counts the trade of the month whether or not it has been paid for.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the shop - the N$60 000 of credit sales are March revenue but May cash, so March shows a profit of N$15 000 alongside a net cash flow of minus N$45 000; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: when money moves against when trade happens; the two figures can differ in sign in the same month.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Swakopmund bakery starts June with minus N$20 000 in the bank. During June its receipts are N$8 000 more than its payments. Explain the difference between the bakery's opening balance for June and its net cash flow for June.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The opening balance is a position at a moment: the cash the business holds at the start of the month, carried forward from everything before it. Net cash flow is a movement over the month: that month's inflows less its outflows. For the bakery the opening balance is minus N$20 000 and the net cash flow is N$8 000, so June is a good month that still ends overdrawn, with a closing balance of minus N$12 000. The difference is a stock against a flow, which is why a positive net cash flow does not by itself mean the business has cash.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the opening balance is a position at the start of the month, net cash flow is the movement during it.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bakery - a net cash flow of N$8 000 on an opening balance of minus N$20 000 still leaves June closing at minus N$12 000; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: a position at a point in time against a movement over a period.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

prompt_replace: State what these figures tell the business.
Explain what these figures mean for the business.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The figures show a shortfall that the existing facility cannot cover. Read against the N$40 000 overdraft limit, April and May are comfortable, but June's forecast of minus N$110 000 means the business will be N$70 000 beyond its facility when June's payments fall due. Compared with June, July improves by only N$2 000, so the gap does not close on its own: the merchant has to arrange about N$70 000 of extra finance, or change the June payment, before June arrives.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the point identified - the forecast shows a shortfall beyond the agreed overdraft.

2 marks (AO2): the figures used - minus N$110 000 against a N$40 000 limit leaves N$70 000 uncovered in June, and July's N$2 000 improvement shows it will not clear itself, so finance must be arranged before June; 1 mark if the figures are restated without saying what they mean for the business.
Comparison and meaning: the balances read against the overdraft limit and against each other, and what that means for the finance the merchant must arrange.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks and narrowed to one point - the June shortfall - applied to the merchant's figures.

prompt_replace: Recommend what the partners should do, and explain what each part of your recommendation does to the forecast.
Evaluate the best way for the partners to improve the partnership's cash flow position.
marking_guidance: 12 marks: AO1 2 (knowledge of the methods), AO2 2 (applied to Kavango Crafts' figures), AO3 2 (what each method does to the forecast), AO4 6 (a developed judgement in context that follows from the argument).
Judgement: a clear recommendation with an order of actions, not a list of methods.
Context: the answer must use the specific facts - 60-day receipts against 30-day payments, three months of inventory, the falling balances and the N$30 000 limit.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the balance falls in every month, so one-off measures alone do not resolve it.
Counterargument: the measures take time to work, which an immediate deficit may not allow.
Condition: state what would change the recommendation, such as the bank refusing a temporary extension.
Each named method must be linked to its effect on the forecast, and the counter-effect of pressing customers must appear.
rewrites.why: Recommend is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Evaluate at 12 marks (AO1 2, AO2 2, AO3 2, AO4 6), the shape of a paper's final part. The ordered recommendation the answer builds is the judgement Evaluate asks for.

prompt_replace: State which of these enter the March column of its cash flow forecast, and why.
Identify which of these enter the March column of its cash flow forecast, and explain why.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and Explain. Four items are asked for, so no single paper tariff is claimed.

rewrites.prompt: Kaoko Juice pays N$96 000 a month in rent, insurance and permanent staff salaries whatever it produces, and spends N$16 on fruit, a bottle and a label for each bottle it makes. Explain the difference between its fixed costs and its variable costs.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A fixed cost does not change with output over the period; a variable cost changes directly with output. Kaoko's N$96 000 is fixed for the month: it is the same at 8 000 bottles as at 12 000. The N$16 a bottle is variable: 12 000 bottles need N$192 000 of materials and 8 000 bottles need N$128 000. The consequence is that fixed cost per bottle falls as output rises - N$8 a bottle at 12 000, N$12 a bottle at 8 000 - while variable cost per bottle stays at N$16.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the total changes when output changes over the period.

2 marks (AO2): applied to Kaoko - the N$96 000 is the same at any output this month, while the N$16 a bottle is spent again on every bottle made, so fixed cost per bottle falls as output rises; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: how the cost behaves when output changes, not what the cost is called.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: An Okahandja workshop makes chairs and tables in one rented building. It buys N$450 of wood for each table and pays N$18 000 a month in rent. Explain the difference between a direct cost and an indirect cost for the workshop.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A direct cost can be traced in full to one product; an indirect cost is incurred for the business as a whole and has to be divided between products before any of it can be charged to one. The N$450 of wood is a direct cost of a table: it goes into that table. The N$18 000 rent is indirect: chairs and tables share the building, so the share a table carries depends on the basis chosen to divide it - floor space, hours worked or units made. The consequence is that the table's direct cost is measured, whereas its share of the rent is a judgement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the cost can be traced to one product or has to be divided between products.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the workshop - the wood traced to each table against the rent shared by chairs and tables, whose share depends on the basis chosen; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: traceable to one product against shared by several, with the consequence that one is measured and the other divided by judgement.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Rundu bakery sells 20 000 loaves a month at N$15 each. Its variable cost is N$9 a loaf and its fixed costs are N$140 000 a month. Explain the difference between the bakery's contribution and its profit.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Contribution is what sales leave after their variable costs; profit is what is left after the fixed costs of the period as well. The bakery's contribution is N$6 a loaf, or N$120 000 on 20 000 loaves. Its fixed costs are N$140 000, so the same month is a loss of N$20 000. The difference is whether the fixed costs have been deducted, and here it decides the answer: a sizeable contribution and a loss in the same month.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the fixed costs of the period have been deducted.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bakery - a contribution of N$120 000 on 20 000 loaves against fixed costs of N$140 000, leaving a loss of N$20 000; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: contribution is before fixed costs and profit after them; a business can have a large contribution and still make a loss.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells 12 000 bottles a month at N$28. Its variable cost is N$16 a bottle and its fixed costs are N$96 000 a month. Explain the difference between its contribution and its level of profit at that output.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Contribution at an output is contribution per unit multiplied by the units sold - what the sales leave after their own variable costs. The level of profit is that figure after the fixed costs of the period have been taken off. At 12 000 bottles Kaoko's contribution is N$12 a bottle, or N$144 000, and its profit is N$48 000. The gap between the two is N$96 000, exactly the fixed costs, so the gap is the same whatever the output while both figures rise by N$12 with each extra bottle sold.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the fixed costs of the period have been deducted.
2 marks (AO2): applied to Kaoko - N$144 000 of contribution against N$48 000 of profit at 12 000 bottles, a gap equal to the N$96 000 of fixed costs; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the two differ by exactly the fixed costs of the period.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

prompt_replace: Set out the steps to draw its break-even chart, and state the points you would plot.
Identify, in order, the steps to draw its break-even chart and the points you would plot.
marking_guidance: Steps must be given in order, and the answer must begin with what is set up first - the axes and their scales.
Inputs: the answer must start from the data it is given - the price, the variable cost per unit, the fixed costs and the output range the chart has to cover.
Each step must say what to plot or calculate, not only name the line: two points for each straight line, and where each one starts.
Result: the answer must finish with what the completed chart shows - the intersection, and how the break-even output is read from it.
A recall card: it asks for the whole construction, which the papers do not ask for as one part, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: Set out and State are not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and kept as a recall card with no paper tariff.

rewrites.prompt: A Walvis Bay printing firm with spare machine time is offered a one-off order at a price above its variable cost per unit but below its full cost per unit. It is also considering opening a second print shop in Oshakati. Explain the difference between the decision that contribution costing suits and the one it does not.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The difference is whether the decision changes the fixed costs. Contribution costing suits a short-run decision taken inside the existing cost structure: the one-off order uses spare machine time, and the firm's rent and salaries are the same whether it accepts or not, so an order priced above variable cost adds its contribution to profit even though it is below full cost - provided regular customers do not learn of the price and ask for it. It does not suit the second shop, whereas that decision brings new rent, staff and equipment, the fixed costs contribution costing sets aside, so the firm needs the full costs of the Oshakati shop set against the revenue it expects there.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the decision leaves the fixed costs unchanged.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the firm - the one-off order using spare machine time, where fixed costs are the same either way, against the Oshakati shop, which brings new fixed costs; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: a short-run decision inside the existing cost structure against one that changes the fixed costs or sets a long-run price.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Keetmanshoop brick maker makes 50 000 bricks a month at a total cost of N$150 000, of which N$60 000 is fixed. Each extra brick uses N$1.80 of clay, fuel and piece-rate wages. Explain the difference between its average cost and its marginal cost.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Average cost is total cost divided by output - the share of the total each unit carries at that output, fixed costs included. Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, which at AS is its variable cost. The brick maker's average cost is N$3.00 a brick and its marginal cost is N$1.80. The difference is what each measures - a total spread across units, whereas marginal cost is what one extra unit adds - not past against future, since both can be worked out from planned figures. So N$3.00 is the figure a long-run price has to cover, while an extra order at N$2.50 a brick still adds N$0.70 a brick to profit, provided there is spare capacity and the fixed costs do not rise.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - total cost spread across units at a stated output against the extra cost of one more unit.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the brick maker - N$3.00 a brick average against N$1.80 marginal, and what each tells it about a long-run price and an extra order; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the difference is mathematical, not one of timing - do not reward past against future, since either can be calculated from planned figures.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek craft brewery makes a bottle of beer for N$14 and adds a 50% mark-up. Similar local beers sell for N$24 to N$28, and its customers rate its beer above theirs. Explain the difference between setting its price from cost and setting it from the market.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Setting a price from cost starts inside the business: take the cost per unit and add a mark-up. Setting it from the market starts outside, with what customers will pay and what competitors charge, and cost then tests whether that price is worth supplying at. The difference is which figure is the starting point and which is the test. For the brewery, cost-plus gives N$21 a bottle, below every similar local beer although customers rate it higher, so if it would sell about as many at a higher price it leaves at least N$3 a bottle unclaimed. Starting from the market points to about N$24 to N$28, which its N$14 cost shows is comfortably worth supplying.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - which figure starts the calculation, the business's cost or the market's price.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the brewery - cost-plus gives N$21 against local prices of N$24 to N$28 for a beer customers rate higher; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the starting point against the test; reward the contrast in what each approach risks getting wrong.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: Define profit, giving the two figures it is calculated from.
marking_guidance: 2 marks (AO1): a precise definition - what is left of revenue after all the costs of the period - with both figures named, revenue and total costs; 1 mark for partial understanding.
Precise meaning only: an example is not a definition.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Define at 2 marks, a definition carrying the two figures it is calculated from.

rewrites.prompt: A hardware store in Katima Mulilo forecasts next quarter's sales at N$400 000 and sets its branch manager a sales budget of the same amount. Explain the difference between the forecast and the budget.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A forecast is a prediction of what is expected to happen; a budget is a plan the business commits to and holds people to. The store's two figures are the same N$400 000, because the budget was built from the forecast, but they are used differently. If sales come in at N$360 000, the forecast is simply revised for next quarter, whereas the N$40 000 shortfall against the budget is a variance the branch manager is asked to explain, and something is usually done about it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a prediction of what will happen against a plan people are held to.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the store - the same N$400 000 figure, but a shortfall revises the forecast while it makes the manager answer for the budget; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: prediction against commitment, shown through what happens when each turns out different from the outcome.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: An Ondangwa water bottler budgeted to fill 100 000 bottles in May, with materials at N$2 a bottle and rent of N$30 000. It filled 120 000 bottles and spent N$246 000 on materials. Explain the difference between a fixed budget and a flexible budget for judging its May materials spending.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A fixed budget states one set of figures for one planned output and is not changed when output turns out different. A flexible budget is recalculated at the output actually achieved: variable items are recomputed at the actual volume, while fixed items such as the rent stay at the budgeted amount. Against the fixed budget of N$200 000, the bottler's N$246 000 of materials looks N$46 000 over. Flexed to 120 000 bottles, the materials budget is N$240 000, so N$6 000 of the difference is about price or usage and the other N$40 000 is the extra 20 000 bottles.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - one set of figures for one output against figures recalculated at the actual output.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bottler - N$46 000 over the fixed budget but N$6 000 over the flexed budget of N$240 000, the rest being the extra output; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: what each does to the comparison when output differs from plan.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Luderitz guesthouse budgeted wages of N$96 000 and revenue of N$420 000 for the quarter. It paid N$93 000 in wages and took N$405 000. Explain the difference between a favourable and an adverse variance, using its wages and its revenue.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A favourable variance is a difference that leaves profit higher than budgeted; an adverse variance leaves profit lower. Both of the guesthouse's figures came in under budget, but they carry opposite labels. Wages N$3 000 below budget raise profit, so that variance is N$3 000 favourable. Revenue N$15 000 below budget lowers profit, so that variance is N$15 000 adverse. The boundary is the effect on profit, not whether the figure is above or below budget.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the direction of the effect on profit.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the guesthouse - wages N$3 000 under budget are favourable, revenue N$15 000 under budget is adverse; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the effect on profit, not whether the figure is above or below budget - the same direction of movement carries opposite labels.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.
